title: How would you estimate the yearly revenue of one busy London coffee shop?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "What is the yearly revenue of one busy London coffee shop?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: Sizing a single business, rather than a whole market, is common in cases. The key is a believable number of customers per day. Have a go at your own estimate before reading on.
body:
The question

What is the yearly revenue of one busy London coffee shop?

The approach

Cups per day × average spend per cup × days open.

Tip: Keep your page tidy: one line per step, the running total circled at the end.

Step by step

  1. Cups sold per day: 500
  2. × £3.5 average spend per cup, including food add-ons
  3. × 360 days open per year

That gives about £630k a year.

Does it make sense?

About £1,750 a day: one person at the till serving one customer every minute or so for eight hours.

Check the till and the margin, not just the sales

The estimate assumes 500 drinks a day and £3.50 average spend, giving £1,750 daily revenue. Over a ten-hour opening day, 500 purchases means 50 orders an hour, or nearly one per minute. That is busy but feasible if demand is spread across the day and enough baristas and tills are available. A single short morning peak can cause more strain than the daily average implies.

The average-spend assumption needs care: does £3.50 represent each drink or the entire customer basket, including any pastry? If a customer buying two drinks is counted once, multiplying customers by cups will distort revenue. Be consistent about the unit.

Revenue does not establish attractiveness. Rent, wages, coffee beans, cups, energy and wastage determine contribution and operating profit. If net operating margin were an illustrative 8%, £630,000 annual sales would generate only about £50,400 of operating profit.
